1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, MD 
Administrator  
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P 
Mail Stop C4-26-05 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD  21244-1850 
 
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
The National Home Infusion Association (NHIA) appreciates the opportunity to submit 
comments on the proposed rule: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and 
Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's 
Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities and Issuers of 
Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (“the Proposed Rule”) issued by 
the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and published in the Federal Register on 
April 14, 2026.1 NHIA is a trade association representing providers of home and alternate site 
infusion therapies, as well as manufacturers and suppliers of infusion and specialty pharmacy 
products. As the leading voice for the home and alternate site infusion community, we write to 
share our feedback regarding the proposed requirements for interoperability standards and prior 
authorization for drugs and the potential impact on home infusion therapy access.  
 
NHIA appreciates CMS’s continued efforts to modernize prior authorization (PA) processes and 
advance interoperability standards to improve patient access and reduce administrative burden. 
We strongly support many elements of the Proposed Rule, particularly the advancement of 
electronic prior authorization and standardized application programming interfaces (API). NHIA 
urges CMS, however, to carefully consider how its proposals apply to home infusion therapies, 
where patients are often transitioning from acute care settings and require immediate access to 
 
1 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026) 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
lifesaving medications. Delays driven by PA processes can directly compromise patient 
outcomes, increase costs, and undermine the goals of value-based care.  
 
We summarize our recommendations below, which are discussed in more detail in this letter.  
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
1. NHIA supports CMS’ proposal to extend electronic prior authorization to prescription 
medicines under the medical and pharmacy benefits across impacted payer categories.  
2. NHIA is concerned that, in practice, Medicare’s benefit structure does not align cleanly with 
the two categories CMS proposes – drugs covered under the medical benefit and drugs 
covered under the pharmacy benefit and urges CMS to consider the unique operational 
realities of home infusion providers when designing any new drug coverage framework.  
3. NHIA requests CMS require impacted payers to have detailed and well-defined prior 
authorization processes for drugs that fall under the medical or pharmacy benefit.  
4. CMS should require impacted payers to take steps to assist prescribing entities by forwarding 
a request submitted to the wrong pathway to the correct one, rather than simply denying or 
declining to process a request.  
 
NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard 
1. NHIA urges CMS to require all impacted payers, including PBMs, to update F&B flat files at 
a minimum daily, and immediately upon any formulary, benefit, or prior authorization 
change, to prevent avoidable disruptions in care. 
 
Submission of Prior Authorization Requests 
 
1. NHIA urges CMS to recognize pharmacy-initiated prior authorization as a standard practice 
in home infusion and require impacted payers to accept prior authorization submissions from 
dispensing pharmacies when a valid prescription has been issued by a prescriber. 
 
Proposed Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial in Response to Prior 
Authorization Requests for All Drugs 
1. NHIA supports CMS’s proposal to require inclusion of a specific denial reason in response to 
prior authorization requests for all drugs.  
 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
1. NHIA supports CMS’s efforts to improve prior authorization processes to help ensure that 
unnecessary delays do not impede patient access to medications.  
 
Proposed Requirement to Support the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) Standard 
1. NHIA generally supports the use of RTPB tools to reduce care delays, however we note that 
many infusion drugs can be covered under either the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit, 
depending on the site of care, payer policy and patient diagnosis.  
2. NHIA requests that CMS require RTPB systems to provide decision-support, including 
information on timelines and prior authorization requirements for each pathway, site-of-care 
implications, and patient-specific cost-sharing amounts.  
 
 
Background 
 
In 2024, CMS issued an Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, which made 
improvements to prior authorization processes and required impacted payers to implement a 
Prior Authorization API in 2027.2 This rule applied to non-drug items and services, and 
explicitly excluded drugs.  
After receiving extensive stakeholder feedback urging CMS to extend the requirements in the 
2024 final rule to drugs, CMS is now proposing to do so. The Proposed Rule applies to Medicare 
Advantage (MA) organizations, state Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) 
fee-for-service (FFS) programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and 
Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (FFE). The 
Proposed Rule is intended to reduce administrative burdens associated with prior authorization, 
which often delay or prevent patients from accessing their prescribed medicines. 
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
The Proposed Rule would require impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization for 
all prescription drugs under the medical and pharmacy benefits, utilizing different technical 
standards depending on which category the drug is covered under. MA organizations, state 
Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed 
care entities, and QHP issuers on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges would be required to 
 
2 89 Fed. Reg 8758 (Feb. 8, 2024) 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
support electronic prior authorization for all prescription drugs under the medical benefit. In 
addition, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed 
care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFE would be required to support electronic prior 
authorization for all prescription drugs under the pharmacy benefit, using NCPDP standards 
consistent with Medicare Part D. CMS proposes an October 1, 2027 compliance date for the 
electronic prior authorization requirements for drugs covered under both the medical and 
pharmacy benefits. 
NHIA Recommendation: 
NHIA supports CMS’ proposal to extend electronic prior authorization to prescription medicines 
under the medical and pharmacy benefits across impacted payer categories. Standardizing 
electronic transactions among prescribers, pharmacies and payers and across benefit categories 
should decrease variation in how utilization management is operationalized for prescription 
medicines, reduce administrative burdens, and generally reduce delays for patients in accessing 
medically necessary prescription medicines.  
NHIA is concerned that, in practice, Medicare’s benefit structure does not align cleanly with the 
two categories CMS proposes. For home infusion pharmacies, coverage for the same drug can 
span across Medicare Part B DMEPOS and Medicare Part D—each with its own billing rules, 
prior authorization requirements, and patient cost-sharing structures. Many home infusion drugs 
fall ambiguously between these benefit categories, which could cause a prescriber to 
inadvertently use the incorrect submission pathway. This could cause denials and delays in care. 
NHIA urges CMS to consider the unique operational realities of home infusion providers when 
designing any new drug coverage framework.  
Take, for example, coverage of intravenous immune globin (IVIG). Medicare Part B DMEPOS 
coverage of IVIG is limited to Primary Immune Deficiency Diseases (PIDD), while IVIG 
treatment for disorders other than PIDD are covered by the Medicare Part D prescription drug 
benefit.  
NHIA is also concerned that maintaining separate prior authorization processes for prescription 
medicines covered under the medical benefit and pharmacy benefit may create operational 
challenges at the point of care. NHIA requests CMS require impacted payers to have detailed and 
well-defined prior authorization processes for drugs that fall under the medical or pharmacy 
benefit. In addition, CMS should require impacted payers to take steps to assist prescribing 
entities by forwarding a request submitted to the wrong pathway to the correct one, rather than 
simply denying or declining to process a request. A patient should not be delayed in accessing a 
needed medication due to the complexity of separate pathways for medical benefit and pharmacy 
benefit drugs. 
 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to support an unexpired version of the NCPDP 
formulary and benefit (F&B) standard adopted by the Secretary, for providers to use in seeking 
prior authorization for drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. 
Home infusion pharmacies depend on accurate, current F&B flat files to make time-sensitive 
dispensing, billing, and patient cost-sharing determinations. In practice, payers update their files 
inconsistently—some weekly, some monthly, and many only after internal policy changes have 
already taken effect—leaving providers to act on outdated information. This can lead to multiple 
problems. First, delays in updating drug pricing references may cause under/over payment to the 
pharmacy and can result in inaccurate patient out-of-pocket cost calculations. Also, delayed 
recognition of new and modified HCPCS codes can lead to prior authorization issues and 
inappropriate claims denials. In addition, delays in updating medical unusual edit (MUE) files 
can lead to prior authorization issues and inappropriate claims denials.  
NHIA notes that when F&B data are inaccurate or conflict with Real-Time Pharmacy Benefit 
(RTPB) information, providers are left without a reliable reference. As a result, they must spend 
time investigating discrepancies, submitting live claims to verify prior authorization 
requirements, and repeating adjudication processes before proceeding with confidence. These 
issues occur routinely and create administrative burden, delay patient access to therapy, and 
increase the risk of claim denials. 
In addition, existing F&B resources—including payer portals, public formulary files, and vendor 
data feeds—are largely designed for retail pharmacy workflows. They often lack medical benefit 
integration, site-of-care specificity, and real-time functionality needed for home infusion intake 
and referral processes. 
Providers should not have to rely on claim submissions to obtain accurate benefit information. 
The purpose of the F&B standard is to provide that information upfront, which requires payers to 
maintain data that is accurate, timely, and consistent. 
NHIA Recommendation: 
NHIA urges CMS to require all impacted payers, including PBMs, to update F&B flat files daily 
at a minimum, and immediately upon any formulary, benefit, or prior authorization change, to 
prevent avoidable disruptions in care. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
Submission of Prior Authorization Requests 
When a home infusion pharmacy receives a valid prescription, it should be permitted to initiate 
and submit a prior authorization request without obtaining an additional physician signature or 
attestation. Requiring the PA to be routed back to the prescriber creates unnecessary delays 
without adding clinical value. 
A physician's prescription already reflects a determination that the therapy is medically 
necessary. Requiring a second administrative step leads to delays in treatment for patients who 
are often acutely ill or recently discharged from the hospital, increases administrative burden on 
physician offices, and disrupts care coordination among the prescriber, pharmacy, and patient. 
Home infusion pharmacies have direct knowledge of the prescribed therapy, payer requirements, 
and patient benefits. Allowing them to submit PAs upon receipt of a valid prescription would 
reduce delays and improve patient access to care. 
NHIA Recommendation: 
NHIA urges CMS to recognize pharmacy-initiated prior authorization as a standard practice in 
home infusion and require impacted payers to accept PA submissions from dispensing 
pharmacies when a valid prescription has been issued by a prescriber. 
 
Proposed Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial in Response to Prior 
Authorization Requests for All Drugs 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to provide specific reasons to providers when denying 
a provider’s prior authorization request for prescription drugs, consistent with the requirement 
for non-drug items and services included in CMS’ 2024 final rule. This requirement will assist 
providers in understanding the basis for a denial and effectively taking follow-up action on 
behalf of a patient.  
NHIA Recommendation:  
NHIA supports CMS’s proposal to require inclusion of a specific denial reason in response to 
prior authorization requests for all drugs. This requirement will allow providers to know what 
information may be missing or needs to be submitted.  
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
CMS proposes to update and standardize prior authorization decision timeframes across multiple 
markets to increase access to necessary medicines, in some cases requiring decisions within 24 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
hours for expedited requests and 72 hours for standard requests. NHIA notes that patients 
receiving home infusion therapy services are often discharged from hospitals and require 
immediate access to home infusion therapy (HIT). Current prior authorization processes – even 
when electronic – can delay access to lifesaving medications, as there are no explicit protections 
to prevent therapy delays while prior authorization requests are pending. 
NHIA Recommendation:  
NHIA supports CMS’s efforts to improve prior authorization processes to help ensure that 
unnecessary delays do not impede patient access to medications.  
 
Proposed Requirement to Support the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard 
CMS proposes that state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid and CHIP managed care 
plans, and QHP issuers on the FFEs support the NCPDP RTPB standard. These tools can help 
identify patient-specific coverage and prior authorization requirements at the point of 
prescribing. 
NHIA Recommendation: 
While NHIA generally supports the use of RTPB tools to reduce care delays, as discussed above, 
many infusion drugs can be covered under either the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit, 
depending on the site of care, payer policy and patient diagnosis. RTPB tools do not help 
determine which pathway is most clinically appropriate, cost-effective, or administratively 
efficient.  
NHIA requests that CMS require RTPB systems to provide decision-support, including 
information on timelines and prior authorization requirements for each pathway, site-of-care 
implications, and patient-specific cost-sharing amounts. Without this information, the tools could 
inadvertently add complexity, rather than reduce delays. 
 
Below is an example of a prior authorization workflow in the HIT context. 
Unaddressed multi-provider workflow creates additional delays in PA processes: 
• CMS proposals largely assume a direct provider (physician) → payer PA workflow 
• In home infusion, the workflow is often:  
• Physician → home infusion pharmacy → payer 
• The home infusion pharmacy serves as a critical intermediary responsible for:  
o Identifying PA requirements 
o Gathering clinical documentation 
 
 
 
1600 Duke Street  •  Suite 410  •  Alexandria, VA 22314  •  P: 703.549.3740  •  F: 888.206.1532   
 
o Submitting and managing the PA process 
Key concern: 
• Current proposals do not adequately account for or streamline this multi-step, multi-
provider workflow 
• Lack of electronic integration across all parties results in:  
• Redundant communication loops 
• Delays in documentation exchange 
• Slower PA submission and approval timelines 
 
Recommendation: 
CMS should: 
• Explicitly address and support physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer interoperability within PA 
workflows; 
• Enable seamless electronic data exchange and delegation between physicians and 
pharmacies; and 
• Ensure APIs and standards support end-to-end workflows, not just direct provider-to-
payer interactions. 
These enhancements are critical to reducing delays and accelerating access to home infusion 
therapies for patients transitioning from acute care settings. 
 
NHIA appreciates the efforts by the agency to streamline prior authorization processes and advance 
interoperability standards to improve patient access and reduce administrative burden, and we look 
forward to continuing to discuss how to better improve the systems for patients in need of HIT. For 
questions or additional information, please contact me at connie.sullivan@nhia.org. 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Connie Sullivan, B.S. Pharm 
President and Chief Executive Officer
analysis:
# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** National Home Infusion Association (NHIA); signed by Connie Sullivan, B.S. Pharm, President and Chief Executive Officer.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Provider Association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Trade association representing providers of home and alternate-site infusion therapies, manufacturers, and suppliers of infusion and specialty pharmacy products; leading voice for the home and alternate-site infusion community.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NHIA supports extending electronic prior authorization to drugs across medical and pharmacy benefits, standardized APIs, denial reasons, and improved timeframes. It urges CMS to adapt the rule to home infusion workflows by clarifying medical-vs-pharmacy benefit pathways, requiring payers to forward misrouted requests, supporting pharmacy-initiated PA, requiring timely NCPDP F&B updates, expanding RTPB decision-support, and ensuring APIs support physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer workflows.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026); 89 Fed. Reg. 8758 (Feb. 8, 2024).
- **Standards referenced:** Standardized APIs; Prior Authorization API; NCPDP Formulary and Benefit (F&B) standard; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standard; NCPDP standards consistent with Medicare Part D.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extend ePA to prescription drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Standardized electronic transactions among prescribers, pharmacies, and payers should reduce variation, administrative burden, and delays.
- **Specific request:** Finalize extension of ePA requirements to prescription medicines under medical and pharmacy benefits across impacted payers.

**Topic 2: Medical vs pharmacy benefit ambiguity in home infusion**
- **Provision ID:** MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Home infusion drugs may fall across Medicare Part B DMEPOS and Part D, creating ambiguity in billing rules, PA requirements, and cost sharing. Misrouting can cause denials and delays.
- **Specific request:** Require detailed, well-defined PA processes for medical- and pharmacy-benefit drugs and require payers to forward requests submitted through the wrong pathway rather than deny or decline them.

**Topic 3: NCPDP Formulary and Benefit file timeliness**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Outdated F&B files cause inaccurate patient cost estimates, under/overpayment, PA problems, inappropriate denials, and unnecessary live-claim verification.
- **Specific request:** Require all impacted payers, including PBMs, to update F&B flat files at least daily and immediately after formulary, benefit, or PA changes.

**Topic 4: Pharmacy-initiated prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; EXISTING-WORKFLOWS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** In home infusion, requiring a request to be routed back to the prescriber for an additional signature delays care without adding clinical value.
- **Specific request:** Recognize pharmacy-initiated PA as standard home infusion practice and require payers to accept PA submissions from dispensing pharmacies when a valid prescription exists.

**Topic 5: Specific denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons help providers understand missing information and take corrective action for patients.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the requirement to include specific denial reasons for all drug PA denials.

**Topic 6: Prior authorization decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Home infusion patients often transition from hospitals and need immediate therapy; pending PA can delay lifesaving medications.
- **Specific request:** Improve PA processes and consider protections to prevent therapy delays while PA is pending.

**Topic 7: NCPDP RTPB decision-support**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** RTPB tools may not determine the best pathway for infusion drugs that could be medical or pharmacy benefit depending on site of care, payer policy, and diagnosis.
- **Specific request:** Require RTPB systems to provide pathway-specific timelines, PA requirements, site-of-care implications, and patient-specific cost-sharing amounts.

**Topic 8: End-to-end home infusion workflow support**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CMS proposals assume direct physician-to-payer workflows, but home infusion often uses physician-to-home-infusion-pharmacy-to-payer processes.
- **Specific request:** Explicitly support physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer interoperability, electronic delegation, and end-to-end workflows across all involved parties.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** NHIA identifies technical and operational challenges for home infusion, especially multi-provider workflows and benefit-pathway ambiguity.
- **S14:** NHIA supports NCPDP pharmacy-benefit ePA standards but requests timely F&B updates and better RTPB decision-support.
- **S15:** NHIA directly addresses medical vs pharmacy benefit ambiguity and asks for clearer pathways and forwarding of misrouted requests.
- **S16:** NHIA supports requiring specific denial reasons for all drug PA denials.
- **S19/S22:** NHIA discusses operational burden and costs caused by inaccurate F&B data, live claim verification, and inconsistent payer updates.
- **S20/S21:** NHIA supports improved timeframes but warns home infusion patients need immediate access and additional protections during pending PA.
- **S25:** NHIA supports RTPB generally but says it must include pathway, site-of-care, PA, timeline, and cost-sharing decision-support.
- **S28:** NHIA raises Part D/Part B DMEPOS alignment concerns using IVIG as an example.
- **S37:** NHIA identifies workflow integration challenges across physicians, pharmacies, and payers.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize ePA requirements for prescription medicines under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Consider unique home infusion operational realities in the drug coverage framework.
3. Require detailed, well-defined PA processes for drugs under medical and pharmacy benefits.
4. Require payers to forward wrong-pathway PA submissions to the correct pathway rather than deny or decline them.
5. Require payers and PBMs to update NCPDP F&B files daily and immediately upon any relevant change.
6. Recognize pharmacy-initiated PA as standard practice for home infusion.
7. Require payers to accept PA submissions from dispensing pharmacies when a valid prescription exists.
8. Finalize specific denial reason requirements for drug PA denials.
9. Improve PA decision timeframes and prevent delays for patients needing immediate home infusion therapy.
10. Require RTPB systems to include pathway-specific PA requirements, timelines, site-of-care implications, and patient cost-sharing.
11. Support physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer electronic delegation and data exchange.
12. Ensure APIs and standards support end-to-end workflows, not only direct provider-to-payer interactions.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Home infusion benefit ambiguity, misrouted PA denials, outdated F&B data, lack of pharmacy-initiated PA recognition, insufficient RTPB decision-support, and failure to account for multi-provider workflows.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed access to lifesaving medications, compromised outcomes, increased costs, inappropriate denials, inaccurate cost sharing, redundant communication loops, and slower PA approvals.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Separate medical/pharmacy PA pathways; retail-oriented F&B resources; lack of medical benefit integration and site-of-care specificity; incomplete electronic integration among physicians, home infusion pharmacies, and payers.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No quantitative statistics beyond Federal Register references.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CMS 2024 final rule and 2026 proposed rule Federal Register notices.
- **Examples provided:** IVIG coverage under Medicare Part B DMEPOS for PIDD and under Part D for other disorders; home infusion workflow of physician to home infusion pharmacy to payer.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Home infusion patients, home infusion pharmacies, prescribers, payers, PBMs, state Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHP issuers, MA organizations.
- **Economic implications:** Inaccurate F&B data may cause under/overpayment, incorrect patient out-of-pocket estimates, claim denials, and higher costs from delays.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports APIs and standards but asks for expanded functionality for multi-party workflows, F&B currency, and RTPB pathway decision-support.
- **Patient care impact:** High impact for acutely ill patients transitioning from hospitals who need immediate home infusion therapy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with significant workflow-specific modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, practical, provider-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "NHIA supports CMS’ proposal to extend electronic prior authorization to prescription medicines under the medical and pharmacy benefits across impacted payer categories." - Context: Overall support for drug ePA expansion.
2. "Medicare’s benefit structure does not align cleanly with the two categories CMS proposes." - Context: Medical vs pharmacy benefit ambiguity for home infusion.
3. "A patient should not be delayed in accessing a needed medication due to the complexity of separate pathways." - Context: Request to forward wrong-pathway PA requests.
4. "CMS should explicitly address and support physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer interoperability within PA workflows." - Context: End-to-end home infusion workflow recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports faster decisions and highlights immediate post-discharge needs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on home infusion provider administrative burden and redundant workflows.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central concern is avoiding delays in lifesaving home infusion therapy.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Addresses APIs, F&B files, RTPB, and workflow integration requirements.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Seeks stronger functional requirements for NCPDP F&B and RTPB in home infusion contexts.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Major theme; highlights Part B/Part D ambiguity and misrouting.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports specific denial reasons and better benefit/pathway information.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Emphasizes physician-to-pharmacy-to-payer workflow rather than direct provider-to-payer only.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for coordination among prescribers, pharmacies, payers, and PBMs.
